reader.title: Lonoke night rider case
bases: A1 describes night riders indicted for taking binding oaths to intimidate Black residents ('Took Oaths to Drive Negroes From Community') and for seizing a Black man to whip him in the woods.
Only A1, a short court dispatch from Lonoke, reports the case; no other white or Black paper in the window was found carrying it.

summary.text: The Lonoke night rider case was a 1910 prosecution in the Lonoke circuit court in Arkansas of three men charged as night riders with taking oaths to intimidate Black residents and with seizing a Black man to whip him.
By the defendants' account the man escaped under fire and was never heard from again, and in August 1910 the cases against them were reported continued for six months.
The three men, George Granberry, Vernon Leggett and Frank Reeder, were indicted for "taking binding oaths for the purpose of intimidating negroes and riotous conspiracy."
They were charged with taking a Black man out "under the pretense of arrest" and escorting him to the woods to be whipped.
The date and place of the seizure and the man's name are not given in the coverage.
According to the defendants, the man was made to say his prayers on the way, and when the leader stumbled over a leg he broke away.
He fled "amidst a volley of shots," and the dispatch reported that he "has never been heard of since."
The cases had been set for trial at the term of the Lonoke circuit court then in session, but were continued for six months.
No report of a trial, verdict or of the missing man's fate was found in the coverage through September 1910.

The case reached print as a short Lonoke dispatch in the Cotter Courier on 12 August 1910, under the headline "Night Rider Casrs Are Continued" and the subhead "Is Alleged They Took Oaths to Drive Negroes From Community."
The item presented the charges as allegations and the escape under gunfire as the defendants' own statement, without comment on the missing man.
No other white paper and no Black paper in the coverage carried the case.
